item.title: (1978) Music for 18 Musicians
item.description: At a London lecture in 2010, an interviewer asked Steve Reich to tell the room how Music for 18 Musicians came to be, and he declined: “Can’t tell you a damn thing, let’s put it on.” He cued up the recording, offered his score to anyone who wanted to follow along, and played the opening.

item.title: (1953) "Gee"
item.description: A jazz-toned electric guitar solo lands halfway through “Gee” where the saxophone usually went in 1953 doo-wop records, and that single instrumental choice is the reason historians sometimes call this the first rock & roll hit by a rock & roll group.

item.title: (1958) "Johnny B. Goode"
item.description: A pickup lick in double-stops, four bars of guitar before the band enters on the shuffling twelve-bar, and the most imitated figure in the history of rock guitar is already underway — and Chuck Berry did not write it.

item.title: (1960) "Will You Love Me Tomorrow"
item.description: Will you still love me tomorrow? The whole record is that one question, and in 1960 it was a daring thing to sing out loud.

item.title: (1963) "Be My Baby"
item.description: The most perfect pop single ever recorded, or at least the one with the strongest claim to the title.

item.title: (1964) "Leader of the Pack"
item.description: It opens with a single piano chord struck like a tolling bell, the other Shangri-Las humming a dirge behind it, and then a question whispered across the record like gossip passed in a school hallway: “Is she really going out with him?” What follows is a two-and-a-half-minute radio play.

item.title: (1964) "You Really Got Me"
item.description: Two power chords a whole step apart, hammered through a sound nobody had heard on a hit record before: a torn, buzzing snarl that arrives before the vocal and never lets up.

item.title: (1966) "Reach Out, I'll Be There"
item.description: A solo piccolo opens the record, high and keening over a galloping percussion figure, and for a few seconds “Reach Out, I’ll Be There” sounds less like a Motown single than like the title music to a film that has not started yet.

item.title: (1966) "You Can't Hurry Love"
item.description: James Jamerson’s bass enters bouncing and syncopated, weaving against Benny Benjamin’s drums, and for the next two minutes and forty-five seconds everything else in the arrangement orbits that figure.

item.title: (1967) "Strawberry Fields Forever", "Penny Lane"
item.description: A Mellotron set to its flute voice plays four bars of something that sounds like a barrel organ heard underwater, and one of the strangest, most ambitious double A-sides in pop arrives.
